content.text: {"relation": "MATCH", "consensus_summary": "Sheol is the Hebrew Bible's term for the grave/underworld — the common, shadowy, silent realm or state of the dead to which righteous and wicked alike descend, corresponding to NT Hades, distinct from Gehenna (final punishment), and ultimately emptied and destroyed (Rev 20). The consensus notes genuine dispute over the anthropology of the dead there (conscious intermediate state vs. unconscious 'soul sleep' vs. divided compartments), while agreeing on the core referent.", "book_summary": "Sheol is 'the demanding place' (from sha'al, to demand): death's claim on all flesh, swallowing righteous and wicked alike, poetically personified with mouth, gates, and bars. Its dead sleep in silence until it is compelled to give them back at resurrection, after which Sheol itself is destroyed (Hos 13:14; Rev 20:13-14). It is explicitly distinct from Gehenna, the judgment.", "consensus_core_identification": "The common realm/state of the dead — the grave or underworld receiving all the dead, not a place of final fiery punishment, distinct from Gehenna, and destined to yield up its dead and be destroyed.", "book_core_identification": "The grave/realm of death claiming all flesh (righteous and wicked), where the dead sleep in silence until raised, then itself destroyed; distinct from Gehenna the judgment.", "core_relation": "EQUIVALENT", "extension_relation": "SAME_CASES", "boundary_disagreement": "None at the level of referent or extension. The book takes a definite position on the one point the consensus flags as internally disputed — the condition of the dead — siding with the unconscious 'sleep in silence' reading (the conditionalist/soul-sleep alternative listed in every consensus response) and implicitly rejecting the conscious/two-compartment intermediate-state alternatives. This is a stance within the consensus's acknowledged range, not a boundary change to the identification itself.", "material_contradiction": "None. Every element of the book's entry — universal destination of the dead, personification with an insatiable mouth, distinction from Gehenna, Sheol giving up its dead and being destroyed — appears in the consensus primary meaning or its explicitly listed common alternatives.", "rationale": "The book's core identification (the grave/realm of the dead claiming all people, distinct from Gehenna, emptied and destroyed at the end) is equivalent to the consensus primary meaning, which likewise stresses the shadowy, silent condition of all the dead, the Sheol/Hades correspondence, the Sheol-Gehenna distinction, and Rev 20:13-14's emptying and destruction. The book's additions — the sha'al etymology and the assertion that the dead 'sleep in silence' — are respectively an immaterial etymological flourish and a resolution of the anthropological dispute in favor of a position the consensus itself catalogs (soul sleep, per Eccl 9:5, Ps 6:5). The personification with a mouth matches the consensus's poetic-personification strand (Isa 5:14; Prov 27:20). Since the consensus explicitly states that agreement concerns the core referent and not the experience of the dead, the book's stance on that contested detail does not alter the identification; the cores are the same and the extensions are identical (all the dead).", "citation_support": "STRONG", "strongest_objection": "The book decisively asserts unconscious 'sleep in silence' until resurrection, which the consensus treats as a disputed minority/common alternative rather than the settled core; one could argue this material commitment on a contested condition makes the entry REFINED rather than a pure MATCH. Additionally, the sha'al etymology ('the demanding place') is a contestable philological claim not supported by the printed citations.", "confidence": "high"}
